description: Manifesto brings science, technology, creativity, and diverse perspectives together to build memorable solutions for NASA Space Apps. We explore AI, software, data, optimization, engineering, and space science. We seek curious, ambitious teammates ready to build something extraordinary.
summary:
MANIFESTO developed Mars Explorer, an interactive tool for planning candidate walking routes on Mars. Users can explore the planet in 2D and 3D, switch between scientific layers, and select a start and destination. The planner uses NASA MOLA elevation data for regional routes and a higher-resolution USGS CTX elevation model for detailed planning at Jezero Crater.

Mars Explorer compares up to three candidates: Shortest, Balanced, and Smoother Terrain. It shows the trade-offs between distance and modeled slope, highlights steep segments, and flags gaps in selected scientific data. For example, when radiation measurements are unavailable along a route, the tool reports the gap explicitly and leaves radiation risk unknown. By bringing route alternatives, terrain evidence, and data coverage into the same view, Mars Explorer helps future exploration teams decide which routes deserve closer study and where additional measurements could improve planning.
details:
Mars Explorer is an interactive mapping and route-planning prototype that helps users explore Mars and compare candidate astronaut walking routes. It combines a 3D globe and a whole-Mars 2D map with a detailed Jezero Crater view. Users can select a start and destination, compare route options, and inspect distance, estimated walking time, elevation change, maximum slope, and steep sections.

The route model uses elevation data to estimate terrain slope and walking cost. It applies a weighted A search and a slope-exclusion threshold configured for this prototype. NASA’s MOLA data provides broad regional context, while a USGS Context Camera (CTX) digital elevation model supports finer analysis at Jezero. The application also displays data coverage so users can see where measurements are available, interpolated, or missing. Geological maps, rover traverses, science locations, and archived environmental observations add context; layers that are not part of the route calculation are presented separately from route-driving data.*

The project’s benefit is transparency: instead of presenting one path as unquestionably safe, it lets users compare alternatives and see which terrain information supports them. This could help explain how orbital data informs early surface-mobility planning and where better measurements are needed. The intended impact is an accessible educational tool and a foundation for future exploration-planning research. Routes are estimates from orbital terrain data, not safety certifications; the model does not account for every hazard, such as small rocks or changing local conditions.

We built the prototype with Python, Flask, NumPy, Rasterio, and Pillow for data processing and the backend, and JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the interface. CesiumJS powers the 3D globe and global 2D map; Leaflet supports the detailed Jezero view. We used NASA and USGS datasets and services. AI assistants supported parts of research, coding, documentation, and testing; the team reviewed and tested AI-assisted work.

Our creative approach is to combine global exploration with local terrain analysis, while making data coverage and model limitations visible alongside the route options. We considered slope, elevation resolution, missing measurements, route length, estimated walking effort, scientific context, and the difference between measured data and assumptions.
